newsitem.title: POLAND: No Poland land sale liberalisation before EU entry.
newsitem.headline: No Poland land sale liberalisation before EU entry.

text.p: Poland, which last year relaxed rules on selling land and real estate to foreigners, will not further liberalise the regulations until it joins the European Union, Interior Minister Leszek Miller said on Monday.
"The liberalisation could take place after Poland is accepted into the EU, if Poles are granted the same land buying privileges in other EU countries," he told a news conference.
Poland hopes to start negotiations on EU membership next year and join some time after the year 2000.
Last year Poland passed a law allowing foreigners to buy apartments and up to 4,000 square metres (4,784 square yards) of urban land without a government permit.
Purchase of farming land still requires a special permit from the agriculture ministry.

The law, which had been a condition for Poland's entry to the Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), was criticised by some political groups. They fear that foreign capital would buy up land and companies, and Poles would lose control over the economy as a result.
But Miller defended the law. "I think it is a healthy compromise between requirements of international cooperation and protection of our national interests," he said.
The law's strongest critic, the co-ruling Polish Peasant Party (PSL), said it was afraid that foreign purchases would boost the price of land, making it unaffordable for the average Pole.
But Miller said no such danger existed, considering the small size of land purchases by foreigners last year.
In 1996, the ministry granted foreigners 1,414 permits to buy land and as a result 2,400 hectares (5,930 acres) were sold, he said.
In 1995, foreigners received 1,208 permits and bought 2,952 hectares of land.
Most of land was bought by Germans, Miller added.

Some politicians, notably from the PSL and the rightist opposition, say that foreigners have been hiring Poles to buy land on their behalf and much more has fallen into foreign hands than the official figures show.
But Miller said he did not know whether this had really been happening and, if so, to what extent.
